To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the chloroplast genomes from the ulvophycean algae Ignatius tetra-sporus and Pseudoneochlorsis marina carry two copies of a large IR sequence, but the two copies of the IR differ in sequence, with one of the IR copies lacking tRNA genes.

1) all ulvophycean chloroplast genomes analyzed so far carry a large inverted repeat, 2) the copies of the inverted repeat are identical in most species, 3) the copies of inverted repeat in the genomes of the Ignatiales and the Pseudoneochlores diverge in sequence.

the chloroplast genomes from six ulvophycean algae (Pseudocharacium, Dangemannia, Chamaetrichum, Trichosarcinia, Pseudoneocharis and Ignatius) have a large inverted repeat that is present in two copies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution and structure of chloroplast genomes, and we have found a new mechanism that could explain the loss of the inverted repeat.
the evolution of the chloroplast genomes, especially the large inverted repeats.
the evolutionary history of chloroplast genomes of the Ulvophycea.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single mechanism of IR loss, but a variety of different mechanisms that have led to loss of the IR in different lineages.
the IR is a dynamic element of the chloroplast genomes in the Ulvales, Oltmannsiellopisdals, Ulotrichales, and possibly also the Ignatiales.
the IR is present in all ulvophyceans and that the IR is lost in some species by differential elimination of tRNA genes from one of the copies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IR is a very dynamic element of the chloroplast genomes and the mechanisms that lead to its loss are not yet understood.
the IR is a dynamic element of the chloroplast genomes that is prone to deletion or expansion, and that the IR is lost by differential gene loss from the two IR copies.
the chloroplast genome of the Ulvophytes is highly dynamic and the IR is prone to deletion, expansion and rearrangement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chloroplast genomes from the Ulvales and Ulotrichales are not as uniform as previously thought, and the mechanisms of IR expansion/contraction in these two orders might differ.
the IR is a dynamic feature of the green algal chloroplast genome that is prone to rearrangements and deletions, and that the IR is not always a stable element of the chloroplast DNA.
the IR is not lost by a simple deletion event but by a complex process that involves gene loss and IR contraction.
